readings.title: Specimen Days: Hospitals closing (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice when Whitman names a single soldier and when he speaks of soldiers in general, and what each choice does.
readings.focus: The last army hospitals, the men Whitman knew by name, and what three years of service among the wounded taught him.
readings.context: Walt Whitman (1819–1892), the poet of Leaves of Grass, went to Virginia in December 1862 to find his brother George, wounded at Fredericksburg, and stayed in Washington for the rest of the war, visiting the army hospitals as a volunteer: he brought fruit, paper and small sums of money, wrote letters for the men and sat with the dying. Specimen Days (1882) gathers his notes from those years with later diaries. These sections, from the autumn of 1865, are his farewell to the hospitals and his summing-up of the men he served. Read on Veterans Day, they name soldiers who came home and some who did not. Douglas and Harewood were army hospitals in Washington; the “rebel cabal” are the Confederate leaders; coppers are pennies laid on a dead man’s eyes; secesh means secessionist, Confederate. Peter Doyle was a streetcar conductor and Whitman’s close friend. Contraband camps sheltered people who had escaped slavery to the Union lines; ensemble is French for the whole taken together.
readings.contentNote: Incurable wounds and a soldier’s body laid out after death of typhoid; prison suffering is mentioned.

excerpt.locator: From “Hospitals Closing” through “Three Years Summ'd Up”; opens “_October 3_.--There are two army hospitals now remaining. I went to the largest of these…”; closes “…camps, I also took my way whenever in their neighborhood, and did what I could for them.”.

questions.prompt: Who is left in Harewood, the last military hospital, by December 1865? What does that tell you about the end of the war for some soldiers?
facilitatorNotes: “Cases of the worst and most incurable wounds, obstinate illness, and of poor fellows who have no homes to go to.” The war ended in the spring, but in December a soldier has just died of typhoid. For these men the war did not end with the peace; Whitman’s plain list makes the point without comment.
evidence: poor fellows who have no homes to go to
a corpse of a poor soldier, just dead, of typhoid fever

questions.prompt: The December 10 entry sets a “glorious, warm, golden-sunny, still afternoon” beside the wards. Why might Whitman record both, and in that order?
facilitatorNotes: He walks to the edge of the woods “to soothe myself,” notes crows, gnats and the smell of oak leaves, then goes in and is “confronted” by death “the first thing.” The order lets the reader feel the shock he felt; recording the beauty is also honest about how a volunteer kept going. Some readers will find the nature passage a consolation, others an ironic contrast.
evidence: to soothe myself with the hour and scene
Inside the wards everything is gloomy.

questions.prompt: In “Typical Soldiers” Whitman says a list of the soldiers he knew “would be like a city directory,” then names some. Why name them at all, and how does the last sentence change the effect?
facilitatorNotes: Naming turns “typical” soldiers back into persons: little “Mitch,” a color-bearer, two officers of the 51st New York, his own brother George with every promotion, battle and prison. The last sentence returns to the general: such regiments are “inexhaustible,” every township “would turn out” such men. A defensible reading: pride in a citizen army. Others will hear something colder in counting the supply of soldiers after a list of the dead.
evidence: it would be like a city directory
the capacity for just such regiments, (hundreds, thousands of them) is inexhaustible

questions.prompt: In “Three Years Summ'd Up” Whitman insists that he “slighted none.” Whom does he list, and what do the three years seem to have meant to him?
facilitatorNotes: Men of every state, Union southerners, “rebel officers and men,” army teamsters, and black soldiers and people in the contraband camps. He calls the years “the greatest privilege and satisfaction” and “the most profound lesson of my life,” and says they gave him his view of the whole nation. Readers may notice how briefly the black soldiers are mentioned, at the end; others will stress that he names them at all, in a time when many accounts did not.
evidence: I comprehended all, whoever came in my way, northern or southern, and slighted none.
It arous'd and brought out and decided undream'd-of depths of emotion.

readings.title: Specimen Days: The million dead (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Hear the first paragraph aloud as one sentence, and ask why Whitman would not break it up.
readings.focus: The war dead, North and South, the unknown and unburied, and what history can and cannot keep of them.
readings.context: Walt Whitman (1819–1892), the poet of Leaves of Grass, went to Virginia in December 1862 to find his brother George, wounded at Fredericksburg, and stayed in Washington for the rest of the war, visiting the army hospitals as a volunteer: he brought fruit, paper and small sums of money, wrote letters for the men and sat with the dying. Specimen Days (1882) gathers his notes from those years with later diaries. These two sections close the war chapters. Between 620,000 and 750,000 soldiers died in the war, about two-thirds of them of disease; Whitman’s “million” takes in them all. Read on Memorial Day, which began in 1868 as Decoration Day for the graves of the Civil War dead, they remember above all the dead who have no names. The places in the first paragraph are battlefields; Andersonville, Salisbury and Belle Isle were Confederate prison camps where thousands of Union prisoners died. Freshets are floods. An earlier section tells how Confederate guerrillas near Upperville, Virginia, murdered wounded Union prisoners and Union cavalry then shot seventeen captured guerrillas in reprisal. A quadrille is a formal ball dance; Plutarch wrote Greek and Roman lives full of revealing anecdotes; flanges are rims or edges.
readings.contentNote: Describes unburied bodies and bones, the prison camps, a dying soldier’s account of mutilation, and the killing of prisoners.

excerpt.locator: “The Million Dead, too, Summ'd Up” and “The Real War Will Never Get in the Books”; opens “The dead in this war--there they lie, strewing the fields and woods and valleys and…”; closes “…much, civic and military, has already been--buried in the grave, in eternal darkness.”.

questions.prompt: The first paragraph of “The Million Dead” is one sentence. List some of the kinds of dead it gathers. What is the effect of joining them all with dashes?
facilitatorNotes: The dead of named battlefields, the “strayed” dead never buried or drowned or washed away, the dead of disease (“the crop reap'd by the mighty reapers, typhoid, dysentery”), the prison dead, bodies in gullies, single graves, corpses in rivers and at sea, and the cemeteries. The dashes refuse a full stop, as if the list could not end; the repetition “the dead, the dead, the dead” turns the catalogue into a lament.
evidence: the crop reap'd by the mighty reapers, typhoid, dysentery

questions.prompt: “Or South or North, ours all.” Whose dead does Whitman claim as “ours,” and is that claim a reconciliation, a consolation, or something harder?
facilitatorNotes: All of them: Northern dead in Southern soil and Southerners in Northern earth, the land “saturated” with them for ever, in “every future grain of wheat.” A defensible reading: a nation made one again by its shared dead. Others will point out that the same sentence names the Confederate prisons as worse than Dante’s hell; the claim of kinship does not cancel the judgment. Memorial Day itself began among Union veterans, and the South long kept its own day.
evidence: or South or North, ours all
not only Northern dead leavening Southern soil

questions.prompt: Why does the section end with “the significant word UNKNOWN” and a question about monuments?
facilitatorNotes: “Unknown” is the one word that marks the greatest number of graves: at Salisbury, 85 known and 12,027 unknown. Whitman doubts that any “visible, material monument” could answer that loss; his own long sentence, and the land “perfumed” with the dead, may be offered instead. On Memorial Day a reader can ask what remembering the unnamed requires.
evidence: what visible, material monument can ever fittingly commemorate that spot?

questions.prompt: “The real war will never get in the books.” What does Whitman think the books will miss? Why does he add that it “perhaps must not and should not be” written, in a book that tries to record it?
facilitatorNotes: The books will keep generals and great battles; they will miss the “countless minor scenes and interiors,” the soldier’s ways, his “fierce friendship” and “animality,” the cruelty he saw recounted by a dying man. He may think some horrors should not be passed on, or that no writing can hold them. Yet he says the hospital part “deserves indeed to be recorded,” and calls his notes “stray glimpses.” A defensible reading: the book admits its limits while doing the part it can.
evidence: the real war will never get in the books
will never be written--perhaps must not and should not be
